extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (esp. moral philosophy/epistemology); readers evaluating claims about innate principles
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and tests for judging whether a moral or practical principle is innate (i.e., imprinted on minds at birth). Includes proposed marks by proponents (e.g., Herbert) and Hume's counter-tests and empirical objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal consent / universality
rubrics_metrics.description: Proponents claim innate principles are those universally known and assented to by all people; innate moral rules should be stamped upon every mind and thus universally acknowledged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume's counter: actual historical and cross-cultural observation shows many moral rules are not universal (e.g., exposing children, cannibalism, practices tolerated by whole nations). Universal consent is therefore not a reliable mark of innateness. Example cases are cited (Greeks/Romans exposing infants; Mingrelians burying children alive; Peruvians fattening and eating children).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally allowed breach disproves innateness
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rule is generally allowed to be breached in some society, that fact is proof it is not innate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes mere occasional transgression (which may occur despite knowledge) from a practice that is generally permitted and publicly accepted: widespread, allowed contravention undermines the claim that the rule is imprinted as an unmistakable duty. Hume uses many cultural examples to illustrate generally allowed breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty / indubitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Innate principles are claimed to confer certainty: they are supposed to give a clear, indubitable knowledge of duty or truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume argues that if principles were innate they would secure certainty (e.g., knowledge of unavoidable punishment), yet people are seen to be ignorant or doubtful, so innate principles fail to deliver the promised certainty in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority and independence (prioritas, independentia)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of Lord Herbert’s marks: innate notions are prior (come first) and independent (not derived from other ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume critiques this by asking whether the supposed marks (priority/independence) really appear in the candidate propositions; if the constituent ideas are not prior or independent, the proposition cannot be innate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity / conduciveness to preservation (necessitas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Herbert's mark described as necessity (e.g., as making for human conservation) — an innate principle should have necessary connection to human preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume questions whether such necessity actually characterizes the alleged innate propositions and whether this mark coheres with the content of candidate principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate assent without deliberation (modus conformationis / assensus nulla interposita mora)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed mark that innate principles produce immediate assent, without intervening hesitation or deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume challenges this by pointing out that many supposed innate ideas are not received with immediate clarity (they vary, are disputed, or are lacking in children), so instantaneous assent is not evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Component ideas must be innate if proposition is innate
rubrics_metrics.description: If a compound proposition is supposed innate, the simple ideas that compose it must themselves be innate; otherwise the proposition could not be born in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume argues that many candidate propositions rely on complex ideas (e.g., law, duty, God, punishment) that are not present in newborns, so the propositions cannot be innate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and determinacy of terms (virtue/sin must be determinate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Innate principles should be expressed in clear, determinate ideas; vague general terms (virtue, sin) are too uncertain to be innate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume: words like 'virtue' or 'sin' cover many contested particulars; an innate principle stated only in such general terms would be of little practical use unless all particulars were also innate and determinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence in infancy and language-independence
rubrics_metrics.description: True innate ideas should be observable in very young children and in those ignorant of language (e.g., deaf-mute), since they would not depend on instruction or words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume argues we do not find the purported ideas (e.g., identity, impossibility, duties) clearly present in infants; thus the infancy test fails for many claimed innate notions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to corruption by education and custom
rubrics_metrics.description: Innate principles, if genuine, should not be easily blurred, blotted out, or altered by subsequent education, custom, or prevailing opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume notes defenders may claim corruption explains divergence, but this reply undermines the proponents' own appeal to universal consent (if education can erase innateness, then universal consent cannot be used as evidence). He also points out that alleged innates should be clearest in those least exposed to corrupting influences (children, illiterate people), which is not observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical cross-cultural test (contrary practical principles exist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation of widespread contrary principles across societies is a test against innateness: genuine innate principles should not admit entire societies holding opposite rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume invokes historical and ethnographic evidence of diametrically opposed moral practices to show that moral principles vary and are often opposite between cultures, which argues against the innate hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue specificity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Proponents who claim innate principles should be able to supply a clear catalogue of which principles are innate (i.e., specify them concretely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume points out that advocates are 'sparing to tell us WHICH THEY ARE'; the failure to produce a definitive list undermines the claim of innateness and suggests selection bias (each sect picking principles that suit it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical efficacy requirement (must guide action as duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a moral proposition to be an innate duty it must be of the sort that can guide action (i.e., be a command), which presumes knowledge of law, lawgiver, and sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume argues that many supposed innate moral propositions are merely general statements and, without innate ideas of law, maker, and punishment (and the particulars of what counts as sin or virtue), they cannot function as innate duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical/analytic principles not evidently innate (impossibility/identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: If principles like 'impossibility' and 'identity' were innate, they should be present from infancy and be the obvious basis for learning; Hume denies this and uses it to challenge claims that even logical notions are innate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hume asks whether infants actually possess the ideas of identity/impossibility and points out conceptual confusion among adults, arguing these ideas are formed and refined by experience, not born with us.
